title: Two Sum
statement: You get a list of integers and a target number. Find the two different positions whose values add up to the target. Exactly one such pair exists. Return the two positions, in any order.

example.caption: 2 and 7 add up to 9. They sit at positions 0 and 1.

idea.sentence: For each number, ask whether its partner (target minus the number) has already been seen. Keep every number you pass in a map for instant lookup.

jargon.plain: The partner value that completes the sum: target minus the current number.
A lookup table where finding a key takes about one step, however big the table is.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: the list, then the target, e.g. [2,11,15,7], 9

vars.meaning: number of integers in the list

rows.name: Hash map, one pass
rows.note: Each number costs one lookup and one insert. The map can hold up to n numbers.

fast.takeaway: The map trades memory for time. Looking up a partner is one step instead of scanning the rest of the list.

stages.title: Empty memory
stages.note: A map from value to index. It holds the numbers already passed.

stages.title: Compute the partner
stages.note: The partner is target minus the current number.

stages.title: Partner seen? Done
stages.note: If the partner is in the map, its stored index and the current index are the answer.

stages.title: Remember
stages.note: Otherwise store the current number and its index, then continue.

edges.title: Same value twice
edges.why: Two positions may hold equal values. The check runs before the insert, so a number never pairs with itself.

edges.title: Pair uses index 0
edges.why: Index 0 is a valid answer. Test for presence, not for a truthy index.

edges.title: Negative numbers
edges.why: The partner can be negative too. Nothing here assumes positive values.

edges.title: Smallest input
edges.why: Two numbers is the minimum. The second one finds the first in the map.

gotchas.text: Writing if (seen.get(need)) is a bug. A stored index of 0 is falsy, so a pair at index 0 is missed. Compare with undefined, or use seen.has.
JS numbers are doubles. Sums stay exact up to 2^53 − 1. Past that, use BigInt.
A missing key returns the zero value, which is 0 and looks like index 0. Use the two-value form: j, ok := seen[need].
int is 64-bit on 64-bit machines but 32-bit on 32-bit ones. Use int64 if values can reach 2^31 and you care about portability.
Insert after the lookup. Inserting first lets a number pair with itself, for example [3] with target 6.

recap.pattern: Hash map: look back for the partner
recap.key: While scanning, ask if target minus this number was already seen. Store each number as you pass it.
moves: Make a map: value to index
Compute the partner: target minus number
If the partner is in the map, return both indexes
Otherwise store this number and its index
